newsitem.title: JAPAN: Plan to scrap JDB seen unlikely to have big impact.
newsitem.headline: Plan to scrap JDB seen unlikely to have big impact.

text.p: A plan to abolish the Japan Development Bank (JDB), put forward by the ruling Liberal Democratic Party, is unlikely to have much of a streamlining effect on giant state-run financial bodies, economists say.

"The LDP's proposal is supposed to be for scrapping the JDB...but at the same time it says a new corporation will be established which will inherit some of JDB's operations... It's hard to tell if there is any underlying philosophy behind the proposal," said Akihiko Noda, an economist specialising in financial and fiscal trends at Fuji Research Institute Corp.
Koko Sato, chairman of the LDP's administrative reform promotion headquarters, presented a proposal to abolish JDB to Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka in a meeting on Monday.
Mitsuzuka said after the meeting that he would take full responsibility for convincing officials of the Finance Ministry, which oversees the JDB, to abide by the proposal to abolish the bank.

The fate of the JDB, which makes long-term interest rate loans mainly for domestic infrastructure projects, had been a focal point of discussions by the LDP's administrative reform promotion headquarters, which is expected to finalise a reform plan for government-affiliated financial institutions by around July 8.

The LDP's reform efforts comes at a time of mounting criticism over government-affiliated financial institutions such as the JDB, which have been censured for being inefficient and straying into private-sector business areas beyond their originally stated purposes.

In order to properly assess the effects of scrapping public financial bodies, it will be necessary to watch how the money saved through such changes is used, said Kunji Okue, an economist at the research department of Dresdner Kleinwort Benson Ltd in Tokyo.

According to the Finance Ministry, government-affiliated financial institutions are due to receive 20.89 trillion yen in loans from the government in fiscal 1997, of which the JDB is due to receive 1.355 trillion yen.

In any case, it will be difficult to drastically reduce the number of government-affiliated financial bodies unless changes are made to the current system in which funds from postal savings and public pension systems are funnelled to public financial bodies, Dresdner's Okue said.
"If public financial bodies are scrapped, where will the money collected from postal savings and public pension funds go?" Okue said.
The JDB's top executive, Yoshihiko Yoshino, said on Monday that the bank views "solemnly" LDP reform panel chairman Sato's proposal for the bank's scrapping.

"We have heard that chairman Sato...has unveiled a plan to the Finance Minister to abolish JDB, and to re-establish it as a new corporation after reviewing the bank's operations. The JDB views this plan solemnly," Yoshino said in a statement.

Yoshino added that the bank would refrain from making further comment as details of the proposed new corporation were not yet clear, and said the JDB will continue to do its best to fulfil its role as a government-affiliated financial institution.
